blocks.x: Mr. Fontenet, would you tell us something about your music training when you were a child, something about your music in your home and so on? Well, music training when I was a child, in my home, I started learning music when I was 17 years old. And as I said, with Vanna Band, Adam Broussard, Herbert McPuldoon and I, we were the farmers. We got a Vanna Band and then Tom Edwards, we got Tom Edwards, Robert Stafford, Pete Broussard, Peter Broussard, that's a brother, Adam. Where did your group meet, Mr. Fontenet, at your home or? At Phillip Shaston. Phillip Shaston, he was one of them too. We met at his home. That's where we started. Did you play mostly here in New Iberia? At that time, at that time, yes. For a few years, we, because, well, in fact, we weren't playing, we only tried to learn music. You had a long training here. That's where we started. For a few years, before we started playing. Well, after you got playing, you did some traveling, too. Oh, yes, we did. We, from here to Homewood, Tribido, Donistonville, and west, we, as far as Columbus, Texas. Oh. Johnston, Houston, Houston, we used to be there regularly, from the Port Arthur, Moremont. How did you travel in those days, in the, bus? In the bus. In the bus? Well, but, before we started making those long trips, we used to travel in the wagon. Oh, in the wagon. In the wagon. In the wagon, and then we, we got promoted to a hang. How long did it take you to, uh, to make the wagon trip, Mr. Fontenay? Oh, that is about, I guess about three hours or more. It's been fun trying to play the job after the trip, but then back again, yeah? It's been better, isn't it? No, no, it's better than that. Well, we didn't, we, we didn't, we didn't feel tired. Ha, ha, ha. I guess we were so glad. The beggar of youth. We were so glad to. Tell me, what was the pay in those days for playing Mr. Fontenay? Well, when I, when I first started playing the Don La Quarter piece. Don La Quarter piece. And you'd go over and wipe it for that. Well, no, we, we, that was around here, we would get full. Uh-huh. But, two dollars and a half. It was after the war, the royal war, he wasn't there. He went up on that price. Uh, how many men were there in this first combo? Seven. And what was the most number of men that you had in the other combos that you played with? I noticed you have ten in the banner band there. Is that the most that you ever had? Yeah. That's the most. What the number of men do you like most or did you prefer most in your general, your combo? Well, it was, when we, we had the, ten it was easier than when we had seven. Uh-huh. Now what was the usual, uh, instrumentation you had there? I think three brass, two trumpets and a trombone, and what, what else did you have there? Three, uh, they had the, three saxes, three saxes, uh-huh. And they doubled on anything? Yeah. Yeah. One of the saxes, he was, he was, uh, he was, uh, double on the bass, drums. Uh-huh. He could get down also. Uh-huh. He doubled on bass and drums. He had four rhythm, three sax and three brass. That's a well-balanced band. There's those men who play violin, in that band. Yeah, they are. Banjo players. He played. He played. Mr. Pondett, you were talking a while ago about riding the Lafayette in a wagon. When did you fellas get your first car? Well, after we stopped traveling in the wagon, we used to rent automobiles to carriers. They charged so much, we thought of buying an automobile of our own. And, uh, Mr. Harry Hall and Mr. Amy Vittery, they were automobile dealers. He spoke to them about financing us to get by a second-handed. They said, if they wouldn't, they had a Dodge. They had a Dodge truck bag, a caja around. They would sell it to us. Uh, if we could put up a certain amount of money. We were doing so well at that time. They lent it to us. We were going for four days. They lent it to us for the four days with understanding that what we would pay someone else for an automobile, that we would put that on a down payment. And our first down payment was $136 to them. After that, every week we would give $25 every Sunday. We were playing in Youngville. And we'd have any games we'd have during the week where we would pay so much. The first month we had this car, we paid them $482. $137. How much was the total cost of the automobile? It was $1300. And that was the second hand? No, it was the second hand. Oh, I see, I see. And the second month we paid $372. Oh, you were kind of bringing that debt down in a hurry. When did they pay back some of the interest? Very much, three, seven, six. They were very nice with us. They got a mind and charge us any interest. They didn't charge any interest? Well, Mr. Hall, he knew me and Robert Stafford very well. And that's the way we got the... He said afterwards, they'd give us this good service, it helped them to sell other cars. They made money by letting us have them. Would you tell us about some of the other bands in this area in Southwest Louisiana that you knew about? Well, you see, they had the Black Eagle and Crowley, and they had the Yelping Hound. He was playing with the Yelping Hound. The Yelping Hound. Where were they from? They were from Crowley. Crowley. Then... What about the V-Doll band? Well, that was more on the other day. A Coyson music? It wasn't Coyson, it was all brass on. Oh? What band was this? V-Doll band. V-Doll band. That's... They didn't play jazz or ragtime music. They had Gabriel from Timidoo. They had... Clever Williams from Donison. No, no, no. It was Stood from Baton Rouge. Tooth Johnson. What was the one from Baton Rouge? Stood and... And Tooth Johnson. Was he a trumpet player? Tooth Johnson. Yeah, what did Tooth Johnson play? Nothing. I think it was his brother. Victor. Yeah. He played violin, I think. Tooth Johnson was from Baton Rouge. Yes. And they had the Royal Band in Lake Charlottes. How big were these bands? Most of them? Well, most of the bands at that time were seven or eight. Did they play a bar like the band? You felt they were better than they were? Naturally. He felt we were better than all of them. And in many instances, it was a problem. It was true. Well, when you had Bunk Johnson in your band, you probably felt y'all had the best band of them all, huh? Well, I'm a mauler. He did a... He did something hard to beat. Do you know of any outstanding musicians from these other groups that finally got the fame that Bunk got? What about Lawrence Dewey? Was he fairly well known? Well, he was. He was in his family. He didn't get the fame that Bunk. No, he didn't. What was the fame that he had in Bunk? Well, he didn't get the fame that Bunk. Which one is that? That's the trumpet player that I tell you about that could play his fame. Oh, yeah. What was his name again? E-Van Thomas. Oh, yeah. Mr. Farnett, what was, what were some of the places you played in this area? Would you tell us something about the dances that you played for? Sure. Well, Sheraton Beach, one of the places we played there Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Sunday. Every other Sunday. Every other Sunday. Every other Sunday. And we played in Youngville every other Sunday. Played Appleville, Erath, Gaydon, Kaplan, Eunice, Opelousa, Generate, Morgan City, Franklin. Homer, Thibodeau, Donaldsonville, Nick Chung, Crowley, Bill Platt. Gee, that was quite a wide area. Would you tell us something about the dances? How did, were there just regular dances? Well, it was, it was regular dances. In, in, uh, Sheraton, well, they had what they, they called a jitney dances. Uh-huh. You would play a number, and then everybody would leave off the pavilion. And as soon as they'd play off the pavilion, you'd start another. Uh-huh. And they'd charge them ten cents a day. Ten cents a day, sir. And they'd charge the gentleman ten cents a day. That was the only place that had that? Well, at Lafayette, once there was a fair, and they had a jitney dance. So, we played another time in Crowley, Franklin. Uh-huh. They had, but most of the dances were regular dances. Well, you certainly did quite a bit of traveling. Play all these dances, all these tongues. Well, at that time, they didn't have, they didn't have these nightclubs. Yeah. We were playing every night. Uh-huh. But today, with all these nightclubs, everybody dancing on Saturday. That's the night, right? Uh, how, how long did the dances last? Four hours. Just four hours? Sometimes they would hire you over time. Uh-huh. When were, you said the dances were,

Almost every night of the week or just the weekend? At that time we were playing every night. Oh my. I guess people really like to dance a lot more than they do now. After they start to be nightclubs, the dances start to fall off. Well that's a surprising statement to make, isn't it? I wonder why. Generally speaking, were the people who attended the dances at this time pretty well behaved Mr. Fontenet? Most of them were. You didn't have to have a floor walk in those? Well, one of two places it was, but most of the places. Everyone just came and enjoyed themselves and danced. There was one man in New York City named Grossman talking about jazz. He felt that there was a big religious influence in that. Do you feel that that is true? I feel that this is something. Can you tell us exactly why you feel that? Is it because you used spirituals in your combinations at any time? Well, the reason I said that during that time playing jazz, especially if you were improvising, you would have to have a lot of people. It's a kind of feeling that you would have. Emotional. That's it. That's it. Can you recall the names of some of the most popular pieces that your group played during the years that come to mind? Do any of them come to mind? Well, during that time, Blackball was one of the numbers. Blackball. Blackball is the one. Peace out. Our name was Smiles. Uh-huh. Now those were popular tunes? Yeah, they were popular tunes. They were popular tunes. Did you play any of the Dixieland tunes also at that time, the High Society or whatever? High Society was one of the popular numbers, was it? Very popular. In fact, it's still popular. Yes, that's right. Was there any special music, let's say, that from New Orleans your group played? Were there any compositions that were popular down there? Well, High Society was one. That's originally in New Orleans. That's right. Did your group ever play in New Orleans or visit down there at any time? With Manor Man? We never played. We had called on two occasions. We were engaged. We couldn't take the job. But I used to visit New Orleans frequently. You knew some of the players down there? Most of the whole. I'd like to ask you this. What did most of the men do in your band and in the band that you know in this area? In what spare time they had, were they particularly interested in anything outside of their music or did they spend most of their time on the music itself? Well, in our, Ed Reedum, he was a carpenter. Adam Broussard was a barber and I was. We had very little time. We had to have someone in the place all the time. Well, just about everyone worked during the day and they played at night. We couldn't do it. We just went to Raglan. We had to have somebody there. We had to work your business for you. We were among you. Sometimes we would leave and deal with it for four days, four or five days. Oh, is that right? Oh. And you had to get someone there to supply for you in your shop. Did most of the men get married that you mentioned being among your group here or were most of them all bachelors? What did most of them? I don't know. They were married. Bunk was about the biggest bachelor. Bunk Johnson? Yeah. He married late on, but everybody else were married. That's difficult. Just going to New Orleans to visit. I met my wife. I didn't meet my wife to me. That's why I became interested in music. One night we went out there dancing. And I don't remember just what band was playing. Thought comes to me that I want to learn to play dance. That's when you were around. How old were you then? Well, I guess I was about sixteen years old. And you started when you were seven or seven. And when did you get married? I was twenty-one years old. Uh-huh. Was your wife interested in music too, Mr. Funday? No. She wasn't interested in music, but she liked to sing. Uh-huh. And that had a good deal to do with helping me to improvise.
She comes from a musical family.

She did? It did. A good deal to help me and improvise. Uh-huh. I tried to improvise. We'd sit on the gallery. Uh-huh. And I would sing the melody of my number. Uh-huh. And she'd make the other part. And we'd continue that until I'd memorize it. Then I'd get her to band. Well, she must have done a band music.
When she started, I mean, the first quart that we knew around in this neighborhood, she was the one that started, I mean, in group singing.
Well, that's fine. Well, who was it you said was a while ago? Was it classical musician? My sister. Oh, that was your sister. My sister.
But my mother's people, I mean, the whole family of them, they were all shit musical. I mean, some instruments, some way, other things that they do play. They were, how many sisters? Huh?
How many sisters?
How many sisters they want? They want letters and instruments, Jack. Letters and guitar. Letters and guitar. And Wilbur plays, that's right, so on the clarinet.
Frankie was a trombone player. George played piccolo. Piccolo? The musical family. Right.
There were five sisters.
And it was something the listener. They would get together and go singing. Those five sisters. And one brother played piccolo. Was your father a musician too?
His mother was though.
He, when our boy started, he, afterwards he said he better let go.
Too much music. His mother was though.

His mother was a singer. Uh-huh. I, I, I did most of my practice in the barbershop. We were, we worked together in the barbershop and every chance I would get, I would sit out and go to practice. And we kind of got on this load. He was, I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. This was, uh. It was my, my, yes. My aunt.
His mother was a singer. She was a piano player and a singer too. Oh, oh, oh.

My aunt. What's your, what's my aunt, you know, she, she was, in a way, she bought the first instrument that I played. Is that right? Right. She, she, she had it with a wonderful voice in the group. Tell me, did you ever at any time invite any, uh, soloists, any vocalists, or outside people to come along with your group? Or was it usually just the men folks that run along? Did you ever have any other ladies along to sing? Or. She sang. You, you sang. My oldest daughter, she sang at one time. I was. He was, uh. He is a singer himself. He's not singing. But he's. Oh, yeah. I was going out of it. Well, that's.
Don't get modest.
I mean, he was the main vocalist for quite a number of years. Oh, is that right? Or was it usually just the men folks that run along? Did you ever have any other ladies along to sing?
Or. She sang.
Or was that right? Mm-hmm. The one that had, uh, you, uh, golden boys, huh? That's what it is, golden boys, huh? Or you a soprano, or a outdoor?
Golden boys, Gus, and Silver Tenor, uh, Shine, that's when they had contests.
What's his name?
Gabrielle, Gabrielle. Gabrielle. Sean Jack.
Uh, we used to have quite a few contests, band contests, two bands.
Don't let me mention my voice because I'm hearing this. That's something that's moving when you can't listen to anything else.
Ha ha. Is it?
Anything else.
Ha ha ha. Then you still play with A.M. What's funny now? Kid. No. Who you play with now? Colton Wilson. No. We. We. We. We. We.
We would be playing more than no catchmen if there were more jobs. Ha ha ha.
How many of your groups now? Still seven? Ha ha ha. Yes.
Some times, but it ranges from seven to eight or nine. I mean, it depends. What the, I mean, the people that we work with, it depends on the number that they want to.
Yes, sure.
But the regular pen was only seven.

Now there's some people here in New Iberia, they are high and they want Dixon. Uh huh. That's when you play anything else, they want to ask you to stop. What style does Mr. Wilson's band, what style do you play in? Well we try to satisfy the people, try to give them some of the present day stuff.
I say that the main style is Dixon-led.
That's why I said we try.
As well as that rock and roll is some kind of knowledge in it.
Do you still play some of the old arrangements or did you work out in years past? Do you try to get some of the ideas in them that you've had in the past? A few. Uh huh.

Especially around the holiday dances around New Year's and Christmas time. That's when they really go into it. The saints go marching in and tiger rank and all stuff like that. I don't think people ever get tired of those tutus.
Do they ask you to play any boogie woogie in any of these pieces here or places that you do you play for them?
Yes we do. And it's mostly among the younger people.
When you find the older set, I mean you don't have that boogie woogie without at all. Is boogie woogie on its way out now do you think or is it still pretty strong?
Rock and roll is kind of smothering it right now if you ask me.
Well I don't think that would be anything that would die out.

I think rock and roll is somewhat on the same footing as this bebop that they had it. It was out in a blast for a while and all of a sudden it just died out. That rock and roll I don't think it'll last too long either. It might but I doubt it.

I noticed some of the numbers on the jukebox now they're kind of getting away from rock and roll some of the numbers. Some people seem to think that rock and roll is less but I don't. It's kind of hard to say. Why would you say that the Dixieland style seems to be the most lasting of all? Is there any special reason that you would have been on? I think I think and there was more music. A musician at that time had to learn to execute his instrument more than the, the, with this rock and roll. Yeah there's not anything very complex about that. And then the Dixieland when they were playing everybody, everybody was awake. Who was better than them? It was competition between the boys. Exactly. That's right. Well that was the style of music I guess we used. That's right. We have to play. That's right. They have us enough to. Mr. Fontenot we'd like to know if any of the white musicians interested in jazz in this area. stuff

around here ever came in and then sat on your combos and their playing for these various dances? No, they didn't. Not out here. Well, how did these white musicians that like jazz, like Dixieland, show their interest in this? They would come to the dances in different places and listen. They would follow you around in from one place to another. Yes. Do you recall the names of any of the outstanding colored musicians that are in this area or in New Orleans who worked with white musicians to teach them how to play Dixieland? Do you know any of those? Emanuel Manetta in New Orleans. He taught quite a few. Emanuel Manetta. 된 !
